name: Stopping distance
seoTitle: Stopping distance Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Stopping distance: work out stopping distance from the vehicle speed and the perception-reaction time. A free physics calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Supply the vehicle speed, the perception-reaction time, the road grade and the deceleration and the stopping distance calculator solves for stopping distance. It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Stopping distance calculator work?
sections.html:
The Stopping distance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports stopping distance in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the vehicle speed, the perception-reaction time, the road grade (slope) and the deceleration.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in kilometers per hour. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in seconds. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as dry and wet. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters per second squared. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Stopping distance calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Stopping distance=((1 ÷ 63500) × vehicle speed × (17653 × perception-reaction time × (road grade (slope) + (-7 ÷ 10 × the road is... + (2199 ÷ 2000) × the road is... ÷ (vehicle speed ^ 73 ÷ 250) + 7 ÷ 10)) + 250 × vehicle speed) ÷ (road grade (slope) + (-7 ÷ 10 × the road is... + (2199 ÷ 2000) × the road is... ÷ (vehicle speed ^ 73 ÷ 250) + 7 ÷ 10)))
Friction coefficient=(-7 ÷ 10 × the road is... + (2199 ÷ 2000) × the road is... ÷ (vehicle speed ^ 73 ÷ 250) + 7 ÷ 10)
Braking time=(the square root of (2) × the square root of (((1 ÷ 63500) × vehicle speed × (17653 × perception-reaction time × (road grade (slope) + (-7 ÷ 10 × the road is... + (2199 ÷ 2000) × the road is... ÷ (vehicle speed ^ 73 ÷ 250) + 7 ÷ 10)) + 250 × vehicle speed) ÷ (road grade (slope) + (-7 ÷ 10 × the road is... + (2199 ÷ 2000) × the road is... ÷ (vehicle speed ^ 73 ÷ 250) + 7 ÷ 10))) ÷ deceleration))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in meters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in seconds, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Speed, opening in kilometers per hour
  • Time, opening in seconds
  • %, opening in percent
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Acceleration, opening in meters per second squared
  • Time, opening in seconds

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Stopping distance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the vehicle speed, the perception-reaction time and the road grade — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Stopping distance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns stopping distance, derived from the vehicle speed, the perception-reaction time and the road grade. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Stopping distance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the vehicle speed, the perception-reaction time, the road grade and the deceleration, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter vehicle speed in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Vehicle speed opens in kilometers per hour and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Stopping distance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
